nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Regency and Victorian stage and the comic journalism of the metropolis
literary_identity: Dramatist, journalist and humorist; the most popular writer of domestic melodrama of the later 1820s and a defining voice of the metropolis's comic press
biography: He was born in London into a poor family, was apprenticed as a boy, ran to sea in his early youth, and then took to the stage as an actor in the minor theatres. He turned to writing for those theatres, and his nautical domestic drama of a sailor's sweetheart, played south of the water in 1829, became the most performed and most pirated piece of the decade, acted with alterations all over the country and in America. He then lived by journalism, and his sketches of married life from a bedpost and his contributions to the great comic weekly made him one of the most widely read prose humorists of the 1840s. He edited a cheap daily paper of wide circulation, quarrelled with the managers of the patent theatres and campaigned publicly against their monopoly of legitimate drama, and wrote plays, essays and stories for the periodicals until his later years. His miscellaneous comic prose was collected in several series, and his after-dinner wit was reported throughout the period. He died in 1866, leaving a son who continued his father's theatrical and journalistic work.
literary_profile: A long list of dramas, melodramas and farces for the minor and patent theatres, of which the nautical domestic drama is the surviving piece; the bedpost sketches and the other collected humorous prose; essays, tales and journalistic writing on the metropolis and its poor. His characteristic method is the sentimental domestic situation treated with a comic, speech-reporting economy, in which the jokes of character and the pathos of the situation are delivered by the same lines.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, point-driven comic prose built on the epigram and on reported cockney and maritime speech; in the drama, workmanlike dialogue, effective stage business and a song placed exactly where the pathos of the situation needs relief. His humour is domestic and verbal rather than satirical in the philosophical manner.
intellectual_concerns: The virtue and the exposure of the poor. The sailor's condition, the press-gang and domestic waiting. The monopoly of the licensed theatres and the interests of the unlicensed stage. Marriage, its drudgery and its comedy, seen from the bedroom and the public house.
historical_significance: He is the central figure of the great decade of penny melodrama and of the agitation over theatrical monopoly which led to the patents reform of the 1840s; his comic journalism defined the voice of the mid-century metropolitan weekly. His best-known drama remains the standard example of nautical melodrama in criticism and theatre history.
major_influences: The nautical and domestic melodrama of the minor theatres
the comic periodical essay of the metropolis
the music-hall and sketch-comedy speech of the London stage
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his boyhood at sea and of his first acting engagements are given inconsistently in the memoirs written after his death.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Irish and Scottish; the anti-philosophical novel and educational writing of the 1790s
literary_identity: Novelist and educational writer; the sharpest woman satirist of rational philosophy applied to domestic life
biography: She was born in the north of Ireland in the middle years of the century, of a Scottish family settled there, and was left early dependent on her own abilities; she spent much of her life in Scotland and in the north of England, supporting herself and her household by writing. Her first book, a satire in the form of translated letters from an Indian envoy observing England, appeared in 1796 and was an immediate success, establishing her name in the Edinburgh and London reviews. The following years brought the great anti-philosophical novel of a family ruined by a system-maker, published in 1800 and much the most effective of the conservative answers to the fashion for speculative fiction. She then turned to education, publishing a long series of letters on the principles of teaching children which was widely used and reissued, together with tales and tracts on the conduct and instruction of young people and a work on the preferences and prejudices of nations. Her later writings mixed educational theory with political and religious argument, and she corresponded with the reviewers and moralists of the day. She died in 1816, leaving a body of fiction and educational prose which her nineteenth-century readers remembered chiefly as a defence of orthodoxy against the schools.
literary_profile: An epistolary oriental satire, a five-volume novel of philosophical delusion, an educational correspondence in several volumes, tales and tracts for young readers, and a work on national prejudice. Her fiction argues by exposure of consequences: an idea is placed in a household and observed until the household is undone. Her educational writing belongs to the Scottish tradition of instruction by development rather than by rote.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, argumentative and deliberately unimpassioned prose, strong on the reported dialogue of doctrinal talk and on the comic exposure of a speaker's inconsistency. Her satirical voice is more directly polemical than that of the contemporary English comedy of manners, and her educational writing is orderly, examples-driven and addressed to parents.
intellectual_concerns: The domestic consequences of speculative philosophy. The education and judgement of children and of young women. National prejudice, the character of nations and the British empire in India. Religious orthodoxy against infidelity. The duties and dependencies of household life.
historical_significance: Her novel of 1800 is the most effective single piece of fiction in the campaign against the philosophical schools and helped end the fashion it attacked; her educational letters were a standard work of the first decades of the century. She is now studied as a central figure of the conservative woman's novel and of writing on the British rule in India before the 1820s.
major_influences: The epistolary travel satire and the pretended oriental translation of the 1790s
the Scottish educational and religious writing of the eighteenth century
the moral-philosophical controversy of the revolutionary decade
biographical_uncertainty: The year and place of her birth are not securely documented, and the chronology of her residence in Scotland and the north of England, and of her family's circumstances, is known mainly from the prefaces and letters she published.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Regency stage, burletta and extravaganza, and the antiquarian study of drama
literary_identity: Dramatist, antiquary and officer of arms; the reformer of the burletta and the historian of English costume and stage archaeology
biography: He was born in London into a family of French Huguenot descent, and was bound apprentice in a City business before he began to write verse and then plays for the theatres. His supernatural melodrama of the corpse-bride, played at a secondary London theatre in the summer of 1820, was the sensation of the season and began a decade of vampiric competition between the houses, and he went on to write burletta, farce, historical drama and the short classical burlesque for which he is best remembered. He superintended stage costume with an antiquary's accuracy, took an active part in the reform of the theatre after the patents crisis of the 1840s, and wrote a notable tract on the condition of the drama. He was appointed to the heralds' college and rose to a king at arms' place, edited ancient romances and chronicles for the societies, and published a nine-volume collection of his plays with a history of the Irish stage and his autobiography. He died in 1880, having been one of the most durable of Victorian men of letters.
literary_profile: Melodrama, burletta, extravaganza, farce, historical play and classical burlesque in a long series running from the last years of the George III reign into the 1870s; a considerable body of antiquarian writing on costume, heraldry, monuments and the stage; editorial work on early English romance and chronicle; and an autobiography. He is credited with the deliberate reform of the burletta into a lighter, literary form and with introducing archaeological accuracy into stage costume.
stylistic_characteristics: A neat, literate and often rhymed dialogue, with a fondness for the anapaestic and the short lyric measure used in the extravaganza. His stage writing is brisk and allusive, treating supernatural machinery with a knowing lightness, and his antiquarian prose is precise, descriptive and illustrative.
intellectual_concerns: The archaeology of the dress and appointment of the stage. The literary reform of the small musical drama. The monopoly, licensing and condition of the theatres. The transmission of early romance and chronicle, and the antiquities of the British islands.
historical_significance: His vampire melodrama fixed the stage iconography of the undead and is the pivot of the decade's supernatural drama; his antiquarian work on costume and the stage founded the modern archaeological study of the English theatre, and his extravaganza is the origin of the classical burlesque tradition of the mid-century.
major_influences: The French melodrame and the comic opera of the Parisian boulevards
the Regency burletta and its managers
the antiquarian societies and their studies of costume and monument
biographical_uncertainty: The date of his first printed verse and of his earliest unacted dramas is uncertain, and the extent of his alterations to his own texts in the collected edition makes the relation of print to performance difficult to fix.

pseudonyms: The Author of Sense and Sensibility
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the novel of manners of the Romantic decade
literary_identity: Novelist; the principal English prose satirist of manners between the 1790s and the 1810s
biography: She was born at the rectory of Steventon, where her father was the incumbent, the eighth child of a large clerical family, and she grew up in a household of reading, translation, theatre and joke-telling. From childhood she wrote for family entertainment: the early notebook writings of the 1790s, including an epistolary novel and a burlesque history, were performed and circulated among her brothers and sisters. The family's moves to Bath, to Southampton and finally to Chawton interrupted and then resumed her revision of the three novels she had drafted in the 1790s. Her father negotiated the publication of Sense and Sensibility in 1811 and her remaining novels followed with little public fame; she had no income of her own and published anonymously throughout her life. She died at Winchester in 1817, soon after completing her last novel, and a posthumous pair of novels with a biographical notice appeared in 1818, after which she disappeared from the English novel for half a century. Her manuscripts, letters and family papers survived through her sisters and nephews and were edited in the later nineteenth century.
literary_profile: Six completed novels, an early fragmentary and burlesque juvenilia, a short epistolary novel and a juvenilia history, all written between the mid-1790s and 1817. Her subject is consistently the marriage market of the provincial gentry and the moral education of a young woman whose judgement is tested against flattery, family pressure and her own feelings. Her method is concentrated: few characters, one district, a short period, and a plot advanced almost wholly by conversation, letter and misinterpretation. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published posthumously.
stylistic_characteristics: Free indirect discourse used to shade irony and sympathy without comment. Epigrammatic sententious openings and closings. Dialogue so patterned that character is exposed by speech rhythm rather than description. A sparing narrative voice whose moral weight falls on the qualifications of a single word. And a prosody of ordinary English speech carried in balanced clauses.
intellectual_concerns: The morality of prudence and the cost of self-deception; the education of feeling and its exposure to flattery. The economics of marriage, entail, living and dependence; the authority of family, rank and place. The claims of constancy against first impressions; the limits of sympathy and the difficulty of self-knowledge. The suspicion of novels and of the Gothic as a model of mind.
historical_significance: She transformed the eighteenth-century comedy of manners into a modern analytic prose fiction, and her technical example - the use of a limited intelligence and of reported speech as the instrument of moral judgement - established the line of English realism that the later nineteenth century took as its beginning. Her rehabilitation from Victorian obscurity made her the most continuously critiqued English novelist, and her work is now central to study of the period's sexual, economic and literary history.
major_influences: Samuel Johnson
Frances Burney
Ann Radcliffe
the eighteenth-century novel of character
the family theatre and charade tradition
biographical_uncertainty: Her working chronology is contested in detail: the first-draft dates of the early novels, the order of revision, and the extent of the 1809-1817 recasting are argued from the family memoranda and her own letters rather than fixed by external record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the tragedy of the passions and the dramatic verse of the Romantic decade
literary_identity: Tragic dramatist and poet; the most serious English-language woman dramatist of the age and the theorist of the analysis of a single passion
biography: She was the daughter of a Scottish university teacher of divinity and grew up in the Lanarkshire manse before the family removed to Glasgow and then to London, where her brother became one of the most distinguished physicians of the day. She was formed by a long private reading in the old drama and in Greek and modern tragedy rather than by the theatre itself, and she wrote from early womanhood with the plan of a series of plays each founded on one passion analysed in its progress. The first series appeared by subscription in 1798 and was praised by the most influential critic of the age as the work of a serious tragic mind; two further instalments of the series followed in the next fifteen years, and one tragedy of the number, of a man consumed by hatred, was acted at the patent theatre and held the stage with great success in the 1820s. She published a volume of dramatic and descriptive verse and a tragedy attempted at Drury Lane which failed in spite of management support, and she wrote much occasional and ballad verse for the annuals. She never married, lived with her brother and his family and afterwards in her own house in north London, and became the centre of a long literary circle of visitors and correspondents. She died in 1851 at Hampstead, leaving unpublished papers.
literary_profile: A planned series of plays on the passions, issued in several volumes over fourteen years, of which the tragedy of hatred is the enduring piece; a volume of metrical sketches and descriptive and occasional verse; a ballad and legend of the Scottish past; and an important preface and argument setting out the theory of the single-passion analysis. Her dramaturgy is analytic and rhetorical, built on soliloquy and on the progressive disclosure of one governing feeling rather than on incident.
stylistic_characteristics: Correct and sustained blank verse, closer to the eighteenth-century school of tragedy than to the looser practice of her contemporaries, with a strong use of sententious generalisation and of the interrupted speech of self-examination. Her prose argument is plain and methodical, and her ballad and descriptive verse is quieter and more colloquial than her tragedy.
intellectual_concerns: The anatomy of the passions and their tyrannical progress. The obligations and injuries of family and benefaction. Revenge, hatred and their effect on the mind that harbours them. The responsibility of the dramatist to moral philosophy. Women's authority in the serious drama and the difficulty of the stage for a woman's writing.
historical_significance: She is the principal tragic poet of the Romantic period who was also a woman, and her series is the most systematic attempt of the age to unite the moral-philosophical analysis of the passions with regular drama. The successful revival of her best play by a famous actor of the 1820s gave her a place in the acting repertory, and her theoretical preface remains a key document of Romantic dramatic thought.
major_influences: The Greek tragedy of character
the Elizabethan and early modern drama of passion
the moral-philosophical analysis of the feelings
the Scottish ballad and legend
biographical_uncertainty: The date at which the several plays of the series were composed is uncertain, since the published volumes were assembled from a much longer period of writing, and the extent of her brother's household's influence on her publication is imperfectly documented.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; radical Romanticism and the philosophical and Gothic novel of the 1810s and 1820s
literary_identity: Novelist, biographer and editor; the creator of modern scientific romance and the chief prose fiction writer of the second generation of Romantic radicalism
biography: She was the daughter of the philosophical writer on political justice and of the author of the vindication of the rights of woman, who died shortly after her birth; she was named for her mother and grew up in the father's house under the care of a stepmother whom she did not love. Her education was the extraordinary one of the Godwin library and circle, and in her teens she was visited by the poet who was to become her husband; in 1814 she left England with him, and the years of poverty, travel and the deaths of two children followed. In 1816, on the shore of a Swiss lake with other writers, a company of ghost-telling produced the first sketch of her tale of the made creature, which she enlarged into her first novel, published anonymously in 1818. Her husband drowned in Italy in 1822, leaving her with a young son and the task of editing and establishing his reputation, on which she worked for the rest of her life. She returned to England in 1823, wrote novels of historical and domestic calamity through the 1820s and 1830s, revised her first tale with a new preface in 1831 under her own name, and contributed tales, travel writing, biographical articles for a cabinet cyclopaedia and the memoranda to her husband's poems. She died in London in 1851, having spent her later years as a literary executrix of the Romantic movement.
literary_profile: Four completed novels of increasing historical and domestic reach, from the tale of the made creature to the plague ending of the last man, the romance of a pretended plantagenet prince and the study of a failed marriage; an unfinished novel; collections of tales and travel; and a lifetime's editorial work on the poetry and prose of her husband. Her fiction consistently places an ambitious solitary intellect in a world of family and obligation, and treats creation, pursuit and abandonment as moral problems rather than as machinery.
stylistic_characteristics: A framed, embedded and epistolary narration which withholds the central disclosure until the last pages of its first books. A prose of lucid, restrained emotional report, with a powerful command of landscape as moral state. A tendency to argue by situation rather than by dialogue. And in the late fiction a plain, domestic realism quite unlike the Gothic opening.
intellectual_concerns: The responsibility of the maker; the claims and the desertion of family. The education of the sensitive being by society; ambition, guilt and the pursuit that follows. Epidemic and the end of political order; historical injustice and the rights of the disinherited. Women's confinement and choice.
historical_significance: Her first novel founded science fiction and remains the most endlessly adapted and quoted prose fiction of the Romantic period; her last man is the origin of the modern plague and post-apocalypse narrative. Her editorial and biographical work determined the shape in which the second generation of Romantics was transmitted to the nineteenth century, and her fiction is now central to study of the period's science, philosophy and gender.
major_influences: Her father's philosophical fiction
her mother's political writing
the poet she married and the circle of his poems
the Gothic romance of the 1790s
the alchemical and scientific reading of 1814-16
the French historical romance
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of her husband's hand in the first draft of her earliest tale, and the dating of the 1816 sketch and the 1817 enlargement, are contested; her own journals and family papers have been edited and, in some accounts, altered.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the ballad revival and the historical novel
literary_identity: Poet, editor, novelist and lawyer; the defining figure of Scottish Romantic writing and the creator of the modern historical novel
biography: He was born in Edinburgh, the son of a Writer to the Signet, and a childhood attack of paralysis left him permanently lame and given to reading and to the oral traditions of the household and of the Borders. He was admitted to the Scottish bar and served for many years as sheriff-deputy of Midlothian, a post that paid for the life at Abbotsford he built up from 1811. In youth he gathered Border ballads, made translations from German romance and ballad sources, and printed the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, which established his reputation as an editor of native poetry. Narrative poems beginning with the lay of the border minstrel made him the most widely read English-language poet of the wartime decade until the prose romance appeared to occupy the ground his poetry had won. The publishing catastrophe of 1826, in which the firm in which he was involved failed, obliged him to pay the creditors by writing fiction at enormous rate under the pseudonym of the editor of the Waverley romance, and the later novels were produced to that public debt. He travelled in France and on the continent in his last years, was created a baronet in 1820, and died at Abbotsford shortly after returning from Italy, leaving his journals and his debt discharged by the novels.
literary_profile: An editorial career in ballad and Scottish historical printing; a decade of narrative poetry in romance measures; and the series of prose romances from the Jacobite tale of sixty years since to the tales of the Crusades, the Commonwealth and the Scottish Reformation, with late works in the contemporary and Scottish legal novel. He also wrote drama, a life of Napoleon, a history of Scotland, letters on witchcraft and demonology, and an enormous correspondence. His fiction is organised around the collision of a private, domestic, commercial Scotland and England with public event - rising, trial, succession, religious persecution - and its heroes are typically competent, unexceptional young men carried through history by others.
stylistic_characteristics: Long narrative momentum carried by dialogue and by the dialect speech of a fully realised social lower world. The ballad measure and the romance stanza in the poems, with a striking command of the popular fourteener and the couplet. A habit of editorial framing, dedication, preface and note that makes the fiction talk about its own sources. And a moral vocabulary of honour, interest and duty expressed through concrete material detail rather than philosophy.
intellectual_concerns: The mechanics of historical change and the price of improvement; the passing of clan, Covenant and border society into commercial Britain. The legitimacy of the '45 and the problem of loyalty; ballad, tradition and national memory as evidence. Superstition, witchcraft and the limits of explanation; the economics of authorship, patronage and debt.
historical_significance: He made the historical novel the dominant prose form of nineteenth-century Europe and set the terms on which nations wrote their pasts as fiction; his ballad editing shaped the Romantic revival of popular poetry, and his poetry and romances defined the British reading of Scotland for a generation. His account of the interaction of material life and event was the direct ancestor of the historical fiction of the later century, and his career as an anonymous, debt-driven professional author is the period's central case study in the literary market.
major_influences: Allan Ramsay
Robert Burns
Thomas Percy's Reliques
James Macpherson
Ann Radcliffe
Matthew Gregory Lewis
the German ballad and romance of the 1790s translations
John Dryden
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of his anonymous publishing, the share of his printing house's work in the Ballantyne failure, and the date of some early editorial work remain matters of documentary argument; his own posthumous journals were edited and partly suppressed by his biographer, so that the personal record is available only through that mediation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the national tale and the literature of Irish identity
literary_identity: Novelist, travel writer and celebrity author; the creator of the Irish national tale and its most public exponent
biography: She was the daughter of a Dublin medical man and of a family with theatrical and literary connections, and grew up in the Irish capital in the years of the volunteer movement and of the debates on the parliament's future. She began to write for the press and the stage in her teens and early twenties, publishing verse and tales and acting in private performances in the houses of the Irish nobility, where she was admired for her recitation and her presence. Her first national tale, of an Englishman converted to admiration of an ancient Irish house, appeared anonymously in 1806 and made her famous on both sides of the channel; a second, of the Irish Rebellion of the seventeenth century, followed in 1814, and tales of contemporary Irish and Scottish society in the years after the union. She married a physician in 1812 and became, on his baronetcy, the lady of the title by which she was afterwards known; her accounts of France, of Italy and of Spain, written after long residence abroad, were widely read. Her last Irish novels were bitterly attacked in the English press and her reputation declined, though she continued to write and to entertain at her house in London until her death in 1845. Her papers and her autobiography were printed after her death and have been much reissued.
literary_profile: A series of Irish national tales, a historical romance of the seventeenth-century confederate war, novels of contemporary society in Ireland, Scotland and Wales, three books of travel and commentary on France, Italy and Spain, and a volume of verse and of contributions to annuals. Her plot is habitually the marriage of an English interest to an Irish inheritance, figured as the settlement of a national wrong, and her narration is interrupted by songs, legends and told tales which carry the native tradition inside the English book.
stylistic_characteristics: An impassioned, rhetorical and highly demonstrative prose, with long apostrophe, exclamation and editorial pleading on behalf of the injured nation. Her lyrics and simulated translations from the Irish are formal and musical, and her later travel writing is brisk, conversational and self-referential by comparison.
intellectual_concerns: The justice due to a conquered nation and the property confiscated from it. The value and survival of native song, legend and hospitality. The condition of women as the measure of a nation's civility. Toleration, catholic relief and the union settlement. The education of the English reader about Ireland.
historical_significance: She invented the national tale as a form and set the pattern that the historical novelists of the next generation followed in Ireland and Scotland; her public career is the century's most conspicuous example of the woman of letters as a national advocate. Her representation of the marriage plot as political allegory is a founding text of Irish-studies readings of the Romantic novel.
major_influences: The Irish bardic and harp tradition as revived by the antiquaries
the travel narrative of the revolutionary decade
the novel of cultural collision
the drawing-room and stage culture of Dublin and London
biographical_uncertainty: The year of her birth is variously given and her early education is described differently in the family and later biographical accounts; the details of her theatrical and private performances in Ireland rest on memoir written to serve her reputation.
